title: Solve it together: best and worst score
idea: GUIDED via UEPCC. Find BOTH max and min of one list with two best-so-far trackers in one loop.
problem: Test scores are [72, 55, 90, 63]. Show both the best (highest) and the worst (lowest) score.

exercises.prompt:
PROBLEM: scores [72, 55, 90, 63]. Show the best AND the worst.

How many OUTPUTS are there?
options: Two — a highest and a lowest
exercises.explanation: The problem asks for two values: the max and the min. Two outputs mean two trackers.

exercises.prompt: Which two patterns do you need?
options: Max for the best, min for the worst
exercises.explanation: Best = biggest (max), worst = smallest (min). Both are the same best-so-far pattern, flipped.

exercises.prompt: Example by hand. For [72, 55, 90, 63], what are the best and worst?
exercises.explanation: 90 is the highest, 55 is the lowest. These two values are your check values.

exercises.prompt: Plan. How can you get both in ONE walk of the list?
options: Keep two best-so-far variables and update each with its own if
You can't — you need two lists
exercises.explanation: Two trackers (one with >, one with <) updated in the same loop give both answers in one pass.

blocks: Start both best and worst at the first score
For each score: if bigger, update best; if smaller, update worst
exercises.explanation: Start both at the first value, update each on its own rule, then show both.
Start best and worst at the first score, loop, update best on bigger and worst on smaller, then print both.
worst is the smallest, so its test is <. best uses >; the two ifs run side by side.

exercises.prompt: Check. The code prints '90 55'. Your hand example said best 90, worst 55. So...
exercises.explanation: Both outputs match the hand values, so the combined max/min solution is correct.
All equal, so best and worst are both 40. Both trackers start there and never change.

exercises.prompt: Tracking the best and worst in one loop is just two copies of the same best-so-far pattern.
exercises.explanation: One tracker with >, one with <. Max and min are the same idea, so combining them is natural.
